chapter_theme: The impermanence of life (உயிர் நிலையாமை): the life dwells in the body as a king in a drum or a lord over five guardians of a field, and leaves when its summons comes; so praise the Lord, do good, and share your food while there is time.
structure_note: Riddling images of the life in the body and its leaving (188, 189, 193, 194) alternate with direct urging (187, 195, 196); 190 and 191 fault those who do not know the Lord within or see time measured out.

187.reading: Even seeing that all that grows on the branch, with its spreading red shoots and cool flowers, comes to die, they do not without fail praise our Lord's feet; when they are called, they will not know.
187.nuance: அழைக்கின்ற போது (when they are called) is the summons of death. அறியார் may mean they will not know what to do, or will not know him then, having not praised him before.

188.reading: A field ripened for five, and the five keep guard over that field; because a summons comes from the master of the five, the five gave up guarding the field.
188.nuance: The field is the body and the five are traditionally the senses, as in 151. The master of the five (ஐவர்க்கு நாயகன்) may be the life, or the Lord or Death who sends the ஓலை (palm-leaf summons); the verse does not say.

189.reading: There is one drum and there are two cymbals, and the king who lives within is there; when the king who lives within goes out, the drum becomes clay and lies dazed.
189.nuance: The drum is the body and the king the life. The two cymbals are not explained; the two breaths or the two legs are guesses. மண்ணாய் (becoming clay) recalls the clay pots of 143 and 158.

190.reading: Those who don't know the skill of calling it Venkatam do not know the precious life they could bear: the lord of Venkatam, the dancer of Vedanta, Nandi who plays within Venkatam.
190.nuance: வேங்கடம் is the name of the sacred hill, but here it is traditionally broken as வேம் கடம் (the pot that burns, the body), so that Nandi plays within the body. விரகு (skill, the trick of it) suggests the name is a key to be understood. The verse is obscure and the wordplay reading is tradition's, not the verse's own statement.

191.reading: People do not know that the sun, travelling all ten directions, measures out their lives by its knowing; the people of this earth do not stop and perceive it: this is the illusion that holds them, though they know of perishing.
191.nuance: The sun as the measure of life repeats 184. Line 4 (பொன்றுணர்வாரிற் புணர்க்கின்ற மாயம்) is hard to construe; it may say that maya binds even those who know they must die.

192.reading: No one has fully grasped that the strip of cloth, trimmed straight and bordered, will tear; you who see black hair turn white, say that end and birth lie within a single year.
192.nuance: பட்டிகை (a strip, a border, or a written record) is taken as the body or the allotted life. The last line (ஈறும் பிறப்பும் ஓராண்டு) is unclear: perhaps that birth and death are as close as one year to the next.

193.reading: For the pot with its ladle there is one measure of rice, and for the three hearth stones five firebrands; give out the rice before it burns too close; the days let go have already passed on.
193.nuance: A riddle. The pot is commonly read as the body, the three stones and five brands as inner fires and the senses. On the plain reading the verse urges giving food while it can be given; a yogic reading is also traditional and I can't fix it.

194.reading: As a bee that delights here goes to clusters of flowers and drinks their scented honey, so with the state of the life: even if one seeks it with joy and thinks of it, the one who stands in thought beyond the eye of the three lights does not stay within.
194.nuance: மூன்றொளி (three lights) are traditionally sun, moon and fire, and in yoga three centres of the body. Who does not stay (நில்லான்) is unclear: the life, which moves on like the bee, or the Lord beyond sight. The verse resists a confident reading.

195.reading: Considering how things are ordained to come, do good; considering how this earth is ordained to pass, praise the Pure One; if people ask why we need a destiny, it belongs to those able to win the rare gift of a good one.
195.nuance: விதி (ordinance, destiny) runs through every line, set against what one does: ஆம் விதி (what will come) and போம் விதி (what will pass). Lines 3 and 4 are hard to construe and this reading is tentative.

196.reading: Do not stand speaking with envy so that virtue is ruined; do not turn harsh and snatch others' goods; be upright, and when you sit to eat well, give a ladleful first, when you have come into plenty.
196.nuance: அவ்வியம் (envy) and செவ்வியன் (the upright) are the same pair the Kural sets side by side in 169. தவ்வி is a ladle; the gift asked is small and constant, given at every meal.

links.note: The Kural says hunger never touches one used to sharing his food; Tirumular asks for a ladleful given before each good meal, the same habit in its smallest form.

Both make shared food the right use of plenty: the Naladiyar tells one who gains wealth to eat with many from that day, since wealth turns like a cart wheel; Tirumular asks for a ladleful before one eats.
In 167 the dancer leaves the skin bag, in 189 the king leaves the drum and it turns to clay. Both make the life a performer or ruler inside an instrument that is nothing once he goes.
151 has the five who ate rice with ghee depart at death; 188 makes the five guardians of a field who abandon it when their master's summons comes.
Both say people do not understand that the sun measures out their lives, using the same verb (அளக்கின்றது) and the same complaint (அறிகிலார்).
Both take grey hair as the sign to heed: the Naladiyar's wise renounced in childhood knowing it would come, Tirumular faults those who see black hair turn white and still do not grasp it.

187 says that all that grows on the branch with red shoots and cool flowers (செந்தளிர்த் தண்மலர்க் கொம்பில்) comes to die, yet people do not praise the Lord's feet. Naladiyar 17 says youth falls as fruit drops from every tree in the dewy grove (கனியுதிர்ந்து வீழ்ந்தற்று இளமை), so do not desire her spear eyes. One image of the tree shedding what grew on it serves two lessons: worship in Tirumular, turning from desire in the Naladiyar.

193 says there is one measure of rice for the pot and fire for the hearth, give out the rice before it burns too close (அடுத்தெரியாமல் கொடுமின் அரிசி), for the days let go are gone. Thiruppugazh 858 tells the life of a miser who would not let a husk fall (அணுவளவு தவிடு), drove off the ascetic asking for food, and ended on the pyre. 858 is the life that ignored 193's command, told to its end in the fire.

194 begins with the bee that delights here and goes to clusters of flowers to drink scented honey (இன்புறு வண்டு ... உண்பது வாச மது) as a figure for the state of the life. 2097 opens with the same bee delighting among honeyed flowers (இன்புற வண்டு) and says no one knows the honey that enters the mouth unsought. In both the bee's honey-seeking points to an inner sweetness that ordinary seeking does not hold.

195 says: considering how the earth must pass, do good (அறஞ்செய்மின்) and praise the Pure One. Kural 36 says do good without putting it off, for when you perish it is a companion that does not perish (பொன்றுங்கால் பொன்றாத் துணை). Both ground the call to virtue in the certainty of passing.

source_issues: 191 line 4, 192 line 4 and 195 lines 3 and 4 are hard to construe and may be corrupt.
